planting.note: Set out grafted trees in spring in full sun on well-drained soil, sheltering young plants from hard freezes until established.

directions: Sanfilippara is a traditional loquat selection from the Trabia coast of Sicily, prized for pale, white-fleshed fruit with a mild, distinctly aromatic loquat flavor noted in sensory comparisons against other Mediterranean selections. Trees bear heavily in clusters and benefit from early thinning to size up the fruit and reduce limb strain during a heavy spring crop. As with other loquats, flowering occurs in autumn and fruit matures the following spring, so a frost-sheltered site is important wherever winter temperatures dip into the low 20s F. Keep soil evenly moist from bloom through fruit swell and avoid heavy nitrogen, which encourages soft, bland fruit on white-fleshed types.
sources: International Society for Horticultural Science - Acta Horticulturae (Loquat Symposium Proceedings)

common_name: Nespolone di Trabia Loquat (Sicilian Yellow-Fleshed Loquat)

planting.note: Plant grafted stock in spring in a warm, wind-protected site, since this traditional selection is grown mainly in mild coastal climates.

directions: Named for the coastal town of Trabia near Palermo, this heirloom cultivar produces yellow-fleshed fruit and has long been a mainstay of Sicily's loquat-growing economy. The fruit carries a notably grassy, fresh aroma that sets it apart from sweeter modern selections in regional taste trials. Grow in full sun with excellent drainage, and thin fruit clusters by hand to improve size, since the tree tends to overset in warm coastal conditions. Protect from any hard frost during the late-winter bloom period, as flower and young-fruit loss is the main limit on yield for this cultivar outside its native mild-winter range.
sources: International Society for Horticultural Science - Acta Horticulturae (Loquat Symposium Proceedings)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun; this cultivar is the most widely planted loquat in China and performs well in warm subtropical gardens.

directions: Dawuxing, whose name translates roughly as Big Five Star, is China's most extensively cultivated loquat selection and bears large fruit with yellow-to-orange flesh. It is a dependable, vigorous grower that responds well to cluster thinning in early spring to concentrate size and sugar into fewer fruit. Give it a full-sun site with good air movement, since dense canopies in humid climates can favor fungal leaf and fruit problems. Winter chilling needs are minimal, but open flowers and developing fruit are still vulnerable to hard freezes, so a sheltered site matters most at the colder edge of its range.
sources: International Society for Horticultural Science - Acta Horticulturae (Panxi Region Loquat Introduction Trial)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun; this extra-early selection ripens ahead of most other loquat cultivars.

directions: Zaozhong No. 6 is a Chinese selection grown for its large, orange-yellow-fleshed fruit that ripens notably earlier than most loquat cultivars, making it valuable for extending the start of the harvest season. It has also become an important breeding parent for newer white-fleshed selections, a sign of its strong fruit quality and vigor. Give it full sun and well-drained soil, and thin crowded fruit clusters in early spring to maximize individual fruit size on this large-fruited type. Because flowering and early fruit set both occur during the cooler months, a site shielded from hard freezes and cold wind is important for consistent cropping.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in a warm, sheltered full-sun site, since this cultivar is noted for below-average cold tolerance even among loquats.

directions: Baisha is a traditional white-fleshed loquat from Guangdong Province, prized for ivory-colored flesh and a mild, sweet flavor that researchers attribute to very low carotenoid accumulation in the fruit compared with orange- or red-fleshed types. It is best suited to genuinely warm, humid-subtropical gardens, since studies have found it more prone to chilling injury than many other loquat selections. Plant in full sun with rich, well-drained soil, and protect both the canopy and ripening fruit from cold snaps, which can cause flesh browning and surface pitting. Harvest promptly once fruit colors up, as the delicate white flesh bruises and discolors more readily than firmer orange-fleshed cultivars.
sources: South China Agricultural University (Plastid Structure and Carotenogenesis Research)
